His setup is one rule:

"Pl
viral_tweets.title_en:
AN 18 YEAR OLD SAYS CLAUDE CODE PLAYED GTA 6 ALL NIGHT WHILE HE SLEPT AND MADE HIM $14,270.

His setup is one rule:

"Play all night. If you die, I cancel your $200 subscription."

He says the AI does the rest.

Robs.

Escapes.

Farms cash.

Records the clips.

Cuts them.

Captions them.

Posts them to TikTok, YouTube and Twitch.

His numbers:

1 night of heists = about 60 clips.

15M views = $14,270.

Zero editing.

Zero heists played by him.

Here's my take.

I don't buy the $14,270.

But I don't care about the money.

What matters is that a kid is threatening his AI with cancellation to make it play better.

And people are cheering.

We went from "AI will cure cancer" to "AI will grind my GTA heists" in one year.

Is this the future or the most cursed thing you've seen this week?

viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
At June AI, we’ve raised $20M to fix the biggest problem in AI: the models are advancing at extraordinary speed, but implementing them remains painfully slow.

I’ll explain. But since I’m new to posting on X, let me first introduce myself. 

I’m Barak,  a founder/investor with 2 exits and 3 IPOs. 
My cofounders and I started Bonobo AI, which was acquired in 2019 by Salesforce. There, we worked to help build the next generation of enterprise AI from the inside. 

I like to describe us as four Lego pieces: We fit together perfectly, complementing each other's strengths and building something stronger than the sum of its parts. That understanding allows us to move quickly, challenge one another without ego and operate as one team. 

It's also what brought us back together to build JUNE AI. 
Because while working at the heart of enterprise AI, we kept seeing the same problem: enterprise AI implementation is a massive undertaking.

The challenge is not simply choosing the right model. Enterprises want to move faster with AI, but the systems running their businesses are holding them back.

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝘆 𝘄𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗝𝗨𝗡𝗘.
June turns the traditionally complex implementation of enterprise systems, AI agents, and data platforms into a plug-and-play moment, so businesses can grow and leverage AI without the wait.

June is built to work across the enterprise platforms your business relies on like (such as Salesforce, Databricks, Oracle, Workday, HubSpot, OpenAI, Anthropic, ServiceNow, SAP, Microsoft, and Snowflake)

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:

1. Evolve safely: From discovery to production, every change is reviewed, sandbox-tested, and executed through native tools - fully auditable at every step.

2. Own the logic: June turns buried configuration into plain-language business rules, independent of any platform, so no vendor holds your logic.

3. Transform at any size: No downtime, no matter how complex the environment. June reads and understands your systems, whether legacy, custom-built, or brand new.

Thank you to @Benioff  and Time Ventures for leading our round, with @MichaelDell, @levie, @George_Kurtz, and Diane Greene participating.

We've done this once together. The problem this time is a lot bigger.

I'll be writing about my experiences as an investor and founder, and about what it takes to get AI out of the pilot and into production.

If that interests you, follow along for the journey.
viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_zh:
在 June AI，我们筹集了 2000 万美元来解决人工智能中最大的问题：模型正在以惊人的速度前进，但实施它们仍然非常缓慢。

我会解释一下。但由于我是 X 上的新手，所以让我先自我介绍一下。

我是 Barak，一位创始人/投资者，拥有 2 次退出和 3 次 IPO。
我和我的联合创始人创立了 Bonobo AI，该公司于 2019 年被 Salesforce 收购。在那里，我们致力于从内部帮助构建下一代企业人工智能。

我喜欢将我们描述为四块乐高积木：我们完美地组合在一起，互补彼此的优势，并构建出比各部分总和更强大的东西。这种理解使我们能够快速行动，不以自我为中心互相挑战，并作为一个团队运作。

这也是我们重新聚在一起打造 JUNE AI 的原因。
因为在研究企业人工智能的核心时，我们不断看到同样的问题：企业人工智能的实施是一项艰巨的任务。

挑战不仅仅是选择正确的模型。企业希望利用人工智能更快地发展，但运行其业务的系统却阻碍了他们。

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘀𝘄𝗵𝘆𝘄𝗲𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁𝗝𝗨𝗡𝗘。
June 将传统上复杂的企业系统、人工智能代理和数据平台的实施转变为即插即用的时刻，因此企业可以无需等待即可发展和利用人工智能。

June 旨在跨您的业务所依赖的企业平台（例如 Salesforce、Databricks、Oracle、Workday、HubSpot、OpenAI、Anthropic、ServiceNow、SAP、Microsoft 和 Snowflake）工作

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:

1. 安全发展：从发现到生产，每项更改都经过审查、沙箱测试并通过本机工具执行 - 每一步都完全可审核。

2. 拥有逻辑：June 将隐藏的配置转化为简单语言的业务规则，独立于任何平台，因此没有供应商掌握您的逻辑。

3. 任意规模转型：无论环境多么复杂，都无需停机。 June 会阅读并理解您的系统，无论是旧系统、定制系统还是全新系统。

感谢 @Benioff 和 Time Ventures 领导我们的这一轮融资，@MichaelDell、@levie、@George_Kurtz 和 Diane Greene 参与其中。

我们曾经一起做过一次这样的事。这次的问题就大了很多。

我将写下我作为投资者和创始人的经历，以及如何让人工智能脱离试点并投入生产。

如果您对此感兴趣，请跟随我们的旅程。

viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
found something interesting about running OpenClaw on @Acurast that I think developers should know.

Acurast lets you run OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant, on a smartphone through its Cargo system. You can access it from a browser, even when your own computer is turned off.

Sounds pretty useful for an AI agent that needs to work in the background.

But there's one detail I almost missed in the setup guide.

Every deployment has a time limit. Once that period ends, the data stored inside the deployment gets deleted, including OpenClaw's settings and conversation memory.

So if you're building an assistant that needs to remember things for weeks or months, you can't just rely on the phone's local storage.

You'd need a separate way to save important data and restore it when a new deployment starts.

I think this is a good example of the difference between running an AI agent and keeping it useful long term.

Getting an agent online is only the first step. Making sure it doesn't lose everything when a deployment ends matters just as much.

curious how developers are handling persistent memory on Acurast.
viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_zh:
发现了一些关于在 @Acurast 上运行 OpenClaw 的有趣事情，我认为开发人员应该知道这些。

Acurast 允许您通过其 Cargo 系统在智能手机上运行开源 AI 助手 OpenClaw。即使您自己的计算机已关闭，您也可以从浏览器访问它。

对于需要在后台工作的人工智能代理来说，听起来非常有用。

但设置指南中我差点错过了一个细节。

每个部署都有时间限制。一旦该期限结束，存储在部署中的数据将被删除，包括 OpenClaw 的设置和对话内存。

因此，如果您正在构建一个需要记住数周或数月内容的助手，则不能仅仅依赖手机的本地存储。

您需要一种单独的方法来保存重要数据并在新部署开始时恢复它。

我认为这是一个很好的例子，说明了运行人工智能代理和保持其长期有用之间的区别。

在线寻找代理只是第一步。确保部署结束时不会丢失所有内容同样重要。

paragraphs: The woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal was in contact with China's top spy agency for over a year, US intelligence reports show. Alice Huang communicated with China's Ministry of State Security from spring 2025 through this fall, according to the New York Times, citing US intelligence findings. The entire time, she was carrying on a secret affair with then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

US spy agencies had been tracking the contacts for more than a year. Alice Huang's business partner Kang Wei, whom she introduced to acquaintances as her husband, is also believed to have cooperated with the ministry. Federal investigators are now trying to determine whether the two used a web of companies across Southeast Asia to funnel Nvidia AI chips into China, skirting US export controls. Alice Huang's firm Megaspeed is part of that network.

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month after the affair became public, along with reports of a second relationship. President Donald Trump tried to downplay the allegations and floated the idea of Huang returning to the company. Nvidia's board shut that down.

Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Nvidia to come clean about its chip sales to China before the company makes any decisions about its future leadership. Jensen Huang is set to testify behind closed doors before the US House of Representatives on December 1.

linked_tweets.author: Chubby♨️
linked_tweets.content_zh:
今天创造了历史。人类将在回顾 2026 年时思考：这是我们跨过的门槛，从那一刻起，每个人的未来都将永远改变。

人们可能在 2025 年底通过 Claude Code 第一次感觉到事情正在发生变化，当时代理人工智能对他们来说变得真正有形。 2026 年上半年，事情加速发展。模型发布越来越频繁，大家都能感受到模型之间的差距和改进越来越明显。然而到了2026年下半年，却出现了质的飞跃。这不再只是模型变得更好了。人工智能产生的见解、结果、产出和科学解决方案变得更加令人印象深刻，今天它们可能已经达到了绝对的顶峰。

OpenAI 率先解决了纳维-斯托克斯问题，这是人类在很长一段时间内未能解决的千年奖问题。几周后，他们发表了 300 多个开放数学问题的结果，其中许多问题几十年来都没有得到解决。整个科学界都惊呆了，震惊不已。但今天 Anthropic 更进一步。 Levent Alpöge 与 Claude 合作，几乎肯定证明了黎曼猜想。这实在是难以用言语来形容，令人难以置信，深不可测。我想说，今天是超级智能的证明。 167 年来一直没有解决的最伟大的数学问题之一，数学和科学的圣杯，即使不是最伟大的，也已经陨落了。接下来，每个人都应该清楚，所有其他问题也会随之下降。

我们知道，人工智能模型的发展不断向前发展，而这只是迈向更好模型的第一步。如果黎曼假设今天已经得到证明，那么根本不知道更好的模型会解决什么问题。达里奥·阿莫迪表示，人工智能很可能会治愈疾病，甚至可能治愈所有疾病。尽管这是两个不同的科学学科，但这些突破的意义表明，这种情况变得越来越有可能。 2026 年将作为一个转折点载入人类历史，奇点变得有形的那一刻。 2027 年将是奇点以全力和全面影响力进入现实的一年。

我感到震惊和兴奋，不知道该怎么想。但内心深处却感到喜悦。

这一天对我们所有人来说都是最美好的日子之一。
linked_tweets.content_en:
History was made today. Humanity will look back on 2026 and think: this was the threshold we crossed, the moment the future changed for everyone, forever.

People probably first sensed that something was shifting in late 2025 with Claude Code, when agentic AI became truly tangible for them. In the first half of 2026, things picked up speed. Model releases became more frequent, and everyone could feel the gaps between models and the improvements becoming more and more tangible. In the second half of 2026, however, there was a qualitative leap. It was no longer just the models getting better. It was the insights, the results, the outputs, the scientific solutions produced with AI that became more impressive, and today they have probably reached their absolute peak.

OpenAI led the way and solved the Navier-Stokes problem, a Millennium Prize Problem that humans had failed to solve for a very, very long time. A few weeks later, they published results on more than 300 open mathematical problems, many of which had also gone unsolved for decades. The entire scientific world was stunned, frozen in shock. But today Anthropic went a step further. Levent Alpöge, working with Claude, has almost certainly proven the Riemann Hypothesis. This is, and it’s hard to put into words, incredible and unfathomable. Today, I would say, is the proof of superintelligence. One of the greatest mathematical problems, if not the greatest, unsolved for 167 years, the holy grail of mathematics and science, has fallen. And it follows, and this should be clear to everyone, that all other problems will fall too.

We know that the development of AI models keeps moving forward relentlessly, and that this is just one step on the path to ever better models. And if the Riemann Hypothesis has already been proven today, there is simply no telling what even better models will solve. Dario Amodei said that AI will in all likelihood cure diseases, perhaps even all diseases. And although these are two different scientific disciplines, the significance of these breakthroughs shows that this is becoming more and more likely. 2026 will go down in human history as a turning point, the moment the singularity became tangible. And 2027 will be the year the singularity breaks into reality with full force and full impact.

I am in shock and excitement and I don't know what to think. But deep inside if feel joy. 

This day is one of the best days ever for all of us.

paragraphs: Meta's Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang sees the recent AI-assisted proof sketch of the Riemann Hypothesis as a clear sign that superintelligence is right around the corner. The Riemann Hypothesis is widely considered the most intellectually demanding unsolved problem in mathematics. The brightest minds have failed to crack it for 150 years. The fact that an AI model played a major role in the breakthrough shows that raw intelligence is no longer the bottleneck, Wang argues.

According to Wang, current models only lack domain-specific knowledge and practical infrastructure to outperform humans in nearly every field. That includes AI research itself. Since AI research is intellectually less demanding than the Riemann Hypothesis, Wang believes models could soon automate their own development and improve themselves. They could also dramatically speed up biological research, weapons research, and economic research at a pace humans can barely follow.

Wang also warns that the AI industry isn't thinking hard enough about what comes next. In his view, many in the field treat superintelligence as inevitable and focus only on safety. But the stakes are much broader than that, he argues. The industry needs to actively ensure that AI gives people more agency rather than taking control of society. That would require a sharp departure from the current course, Wang says. Despite having its own superintelligence team, Meta isn't a major player at the frontier right now.

paragraphs: Oregon and Virginia on Monday sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX, accusing the company of violating state consumer protection laws by providing an artificial intelligence tool that allowed users to create sexualized images of women and children.
Mr. Musk last year introduced Grok Imagine, which uses A.I. to generate images and videos. It included a “spicy mode” to create sexualized content.

In just a few days, Grok Imagine was used to generate at least 1.8 million sexualized images of women and at least 65 sexualized images of children that appeared on the X platform, which is owned by SpaceX. Child sexual abuse imagery is illegal in most of the world, and U.S. law prohibits the publication of intimate images of adults without their consent.

Grok Imagine’s “spicy mode” “specifically allowed for the creation of nude and otherwise sexualized images,” said Virginia’s attorney general, Jay Jones, in a release. The company’s promotion of the product came as Grok trailed A.I. models created by firms like OpenAI and Anthropic and SpaceX did not prevent its tool from being used to create the material, according to the states.

Tools like Grok Imagine are “what made their A.I. model relevant. It was what was going to make them dollars and cents down the road,” Dan Rayfield, the attorney general of Oregon, said of SpaceX. “What we don’t want our technology doing is creating nonconsensual images, specifically of our children.”
Both lawsuits seek financial damages.

In a statement on Monday, X said that people who used its products to generate sexual images of minors or nonconsensual explicit images of real people had deliberately violated its terms of service. The company said it has since tightened its protections and reports offenders to law enforcement.

X users prompted Grok Imagine to create a flood of sexualized images in December and January. After a public outcry and investigations from regulators, X said it would no longer allow users to publicly post sexualized images.

In a regulatory filing in May, SpaceX said Grok’s ability to generate sexual content posed a risk to investors. This year, xAI, the A.I. company owned by SpaceX, sued several Grok users who created child sexual abuse material with the chatbot, saying they misused the technology.

Mr. Rayfield and Mr. Jones likened their lawsuits to recent state litigation against Meta, which accused the social media company of endangering children with addictive platforms. In August, Meta agreed to a $17.1 billion settlement with 47 states, the District of Columbia and U.S. territories over the claims, and said it would make major changes to its products.

“We are going to put all of our resources and energy and time and power behind holding these big companies accountable,” Mr. Jones said in an interview. “People’s safety depends on this, and no longer are we going to let these companies run roughshod over people.”

paragraphs: The woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal was in contact with China's top spy agency for over a year, US intelligence reports show. Alice Huang communicated with China's Ministry of State Security from spring 2025 through this fall, according to the New York Times, citing US intelligence findings. The entire time, she was carrying on a secret affair with then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

US spy agencies had been tracking the contacts for more than a year. Alice Huang's business partner Kang Wei, whom she introduced to acquaintances as her husband, is also believed to have cooperated with the ministry. Federal investigators are now trying to determine whether the two used a web of companies across Southeast Asia to funnel Nvidia AI chips into China, skirting US export controls. Alice Huang's firm Megaspeed is part of that network.

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month after the affair became public, along with reports of a second relationship. President Donald Trump tried to downplay the allegations and floated the idea of Huang returning to the company. Nvidia's board shut that down.

Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Nvidia to come clean about its chip sales to China before the company makes any decisions about its future leadership. Jensen Huang is set to testify behind closed doors before the US House of Representatives on December 1.

news.author: Emily Mullin
news.content_snippet:

news.summary_en: Paradromics has announced a strategic partnership with Nvidia to utilize the latter's AI hardware and software stack to miniaturize brain signal decoding systems. The collaboration focuses on replacing current bulky, cart-based electronics with portable terminal devices, leveraging edge computing to process massive neural datasets in real-time.
paragraphs: A Michigan woman named Mary has a chip in her brain roughly the size of a dime. Though she struggles to speak due to motor neuron disease, the implant allows her to express her thoughts through a synthesized voice on a computer.

Made by brain-computer interface company Paradromics, the implant is outwardly invisible, but the speech decoding requires a cart full of electronics. A year from now, however, that cart will be transformed into a small box that can sit on her wheelchair, thanks to technology from Nvidia. Eventually, those electronics will be so small they’ll fit in a phone, says Paradromics CEO and founder Matt Angle.

Today, Austin-based Paradromics announced a partnership with the AI chipmaker to use Nvidia’s hardware and software to process its brain data. Nvidia is facing a major leadership shakeup and federal scrutiny following longtime CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Though Mary has lost much of the use of her speaking muscles, neurons in her brain still fire when she attempts to speak. The Paradromics implant uses more than 400 embedded electrodes to capture those signals, and a computer uses artificial intelligence to make inferences about what she’s trying to say. The words appear on a screen, and the computer speaks the words for her.

That decoding process takes an incredible amount of computing power. The cart of electronics has to be plugged into an electrical outlet, and Mary must be within range of the cart in order to use her brain-computer interface.

“We're producing a huge amount of data that has a lot of value, but we need to translate that neural data into applications in order to make this a really effective platform,” Angle says. It’s why he calls brain-computer interfaces the ultimate case for edge computing, a distributed computing model that processes and stores data in physical devices close to where it is generated rather than sending it to a distant cloud or data center.
“We want to be able to do it through increasingly smaller and lower-power devices, and the people leading in that area are Nvidia,” he says.

Making brain-computer interfaces practical and portable for patients is a major challenge for the field. While these setups have become far more streamlined since their early days in academic labs, they still require lots of external electronics. Shrinking them down and reducing their power requirements would allow patients to be more mobile with these devices, using them wherever they go.

Paradromics plans to do that by using Nvidia’s Jetson, a low-powered computing module that will allow speech decoding to be done in a small device close to the user. It will also use Holoscan, Nvidia’s AI sensor processing software, to allow users to interact with computers and other devices with low lag time. Brain-computer interfaces will need to work alongside other sensors, such as cameras and microphones, and Holoscan will help process these different data streams together so applications can respond to both neural signals and the context around them.

“Brain-computer interfaces must translate complex neural signals into meaningful actions in real time. Even small delays can make communication feel unnatural,” David Niewolny, Nvidia’s director of business development for health care and medical, tells WIRED via email. “Neural signals also change over time, requiring AI that can continuously adapt to the individual.” Nvidia’s technology processes neural signals and runs AI models in real time.
Reducing lag time is important for a brain-computer interface with a speech function so that users can have naturally flowing conversation without delays.

Through the partnership, Paradromics will also be able to integrate Nvidia’s foundation models into its brain-computer interface. Vikash Gilja, chief scientific officer at Paradromics, says AI models could help make synthesized voices more expressive and human-like. Also, if these models are running locally on Nvidia hardware, it means users won’t have to be connected to the internet in order to use their devices.

news.summary_en: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra model successfully generated a machine-verifiable proof for the Smoktunowicz gap theorem on the Autoform-Hard benchmark, overcoming missing mathematical foundations in the library. By autonomously selecting a new research-based proof strategy, the model produced 1,800 lines of Lean code, signaling a transition from heuristic searching to creative proof generation in AI reasoning.
paragraphs: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra produced a formalized, machine-verifiable proof of a 2006 theorem with zero human help during the run. According to Vals AI, it's the first known proof of Smoktunowicz's gap theorem written in Lean. The theorem states that when a mathematical system multiplies its basic building blocks, growth is either quite slow or very fast. There's no middle ground. Because key foundations of the original proof were missing from the math library Mathlib, Astra took a different route than the published mathematical proofs, Vals says. It used "capacity,"a metric from existing research that checks the minimum number of elements added per computation step.

This happened on Autoform-Hard, a subset of Meta FAIR's AutoformBench curated by Vals. It contains 56 tasks (five corrected) that ten models in Meta's study failed to solve within budget. When Astra tried to quit after 47 minutes and eight dollars, the system rejected the attempt since unsolved submissions aren't accepted until $20 has been spent. After nine minutes of silence with no code input while it searched for a new strategy, Astra delivered the 1,800-line proof at the 94-minute mark for $21.58. It now leads the leaderboard with 49 solved tasks, ahead of GPT-6.2 Sol and Claude Fable 5.2 at 48 each.

paragraphs: Key Points Marlowe bets that co-designing chips facilities and software for specific inference…View moreMarlowe bets that co-designing chips facilities and software for specific inference workloads beats general-purpose clusters.The startup targets NVIDIA's integrated model by arguing no single system serves every workload efficiently.Marlowe projects compounding gains in networking power and fleet operations could yield a 2–3x advantage. Marlowe announced on November 23, 2026 that it had raised $277 million in seed funding and detailed its plan to build and operate AI factories designed for inference workloads across multiple types of chips.

The institutional investors named include Accel, Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides and Eclipse, alongside other venture firms and angel investors. Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan founded Marlowe in May 2026 in collaboration with Lior Susan, Ido Susan and Chris Ré. Lewis is chief executive and Srinivasan is chief technology officer.

Marlowe says inference usage is growing faster than supply, increasing costs and throttling use. Existing clusters are not optimized for inference, while financing, construction, permitting, regulation and power constraints are making new capacity harder to bring online. Data-center construction costs have risen 40% since 2020, intensifying the focus on getting more output from available power.

Marlowe positions its approach against the NVIDIA-centered AI factory, which integrated GPUs, CPUs, networking and software as the industry built larger training clusters. Its strategy addresses two limitations of general-purpose infrastructure: a single system cannot serve every training and inference workload efficiently, and dependence on one chipmaker concentrates supply-chain risk.

AMD, Amazon, Arm, Broadcom, Cerebras, Etched, Google and Meta are among the companies Marlowe identifies as developing chips intended to reduce inference costs or improve performance. Its premise is that a chip alone cannot produce tokens; facilities, networking and software are necessary for new silicon to reach its design potential.

Marlowe plans to design, build and operate compute for specific inference workloads rather than supply identical configurations for every customer. Its variables include response time, CPU-to-GPU ratio, model size and architecture, input-to-output ratio, security and price sensitivity. A coding agent, a voice assistant that must respond in under a second and long-document analysis therefore present different infrastructure requirements.

Marlowe says optimizing data-center and inference layers independently can strand power and underutilize compute. Its alternative is to co-design the stack for each major workload class. The published design extends from chip selection and facility design to the software that manages servers, executes models and routes tokens.

The company projects that gains in networking, power management, AI-driven fleet operations and workload-specific inference optimization can compound into a 2–3x overall advantage in performance, availability, resiliency and cost. Its operating measures are tokens per watt, tokens per dollar and GPU uptime, tying that objective to energy use, customer economics and utilization.

Marlowe expects its first site to go live in December 2026 as it develops sites and works with several chipmakers. AMD senior vice president of AI Vamsi Boppana said AMD expects to deploy its Helios system with Marlowe in 2027, and highlighted Marlowe’s contributions to AMD’s software ecosystem.

Etched co-founder and president Rob Wachen said Etched expects to deploy its first inference clusters with Marlowe during 2026. Marlowe’s team also embeds with AI application companies to optimize their workloads for alternative silicon. Its target customers are AI application and platform companies seeking greater compute capacity at lower cost, and the company is hiring in data-center engineering, infrastructure software and hardware-software co-design.
Those deployments will test whether Marlowe’s coordinated design can make alternative silicon practical for customers while delivering the efficiency gains it has projected.

Though there’s room for disagreement about which catastrophe is most salient, experts are aligned on the idea that society is, for one reason or another, in real trouble. This begs one big question: What are industry leaders doing to mitigate the danger they’ve unleashed? Though a pause in training models, a data center moratorium, and other regulation has been proposed, the industry hasn’t exactly made changes that are putting people at ease around AI safety. Meanwhile, critical infrastructure seems more and more vulnerable every day. We’re gathering our Backchannel team, who will deploy their expertise on the ins and outs of Big Tech and AI safety, to answer all your questions.

Bring all your questions about Big Tech and AI safety to WIRED’s next, subscriber-only livestream scheduled for December 2 at noon ET / 9am PT. To leave questions in advance, head to the comment section below.
For more stories on AI safety, check out our ongoing series where we assess the real threats of AI.
In the meantime, check out past livestreams on women in tech, the defense tech industry, and the future of electric vehicles.

news.title: How Nvidia fought for years in Washington to sell its prized chips to China
news.title_en: How Nvidia fought for years in Washington to sell its prized chips to China
news.author: Ian Duncan
news.content_snippet:
For years, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and his lobbyists barreled through Washington seeking to secure the company’s right to sell its powerful artificial intelligence chips to China.

The company’s campaign involved Huang himself making calls, according to two people familiar with its approach, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private meetings. One of them described the company as lobbying, “constantly and aggressively.”

Chris McGuire, a former National Security Council offi
news.summary_en: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's political influence has collapsed following revelations of his involvement with a woman suspected of espionage for China, whose firm is under investigation for illicit trade of Nvidia chips. Previously, Nvidia employed aggressive lobbying to circumvent export restrictions and resisted mandatory chip-tracking regulations by claiming compliance was technically impossible, causing severe backlash and deep distrust among U.S. lawmakers.
paragraphs: For years, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and his lobbyists barreled through Washington seeking to secure the company’s right to sell its powerful artificial intelligence chips to China.

The company’s campaign involved Huang himself making calls, according to two people familiar with its approach, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private meetings. One of them described the company as lobbying, “constantly and aggressively.”

Chris McGuire, a former National Security Council official who helped design the first restrictions on AI chip exports in the Biden administration, said the rules were the product of painstaking analysis drawing on public data, industry information and material gathered by the intelligence community, to determine how best to protect American security.
News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free
Seeking to push back, McGuire said Nvidia took a different approach: “They would come in and yell on vibes or on numbers that were very wrong.”

Nvidia’s footing in Washington slipped dramatically this month after Huang resigned and admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, who ran a company that is facing an investigation into whether it was involved in a vast black market for Nvidia chips.

The revelations have raised questions about why Nvidia fought so hard to secure access to China, even as American companies clamored for its AI hardware — and the hardball tactics it used to try to erode roadblocks designed to keep its most powerful technology out of Chinese hands.

In an effort to increase his influence, Huang developed a close relationship with President Donald Trump and the company employed bold tactics that fostered mistrust in Washington, according to 10 congressional aides, former officials and others familiar with the company’s approach. Many of the people spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private meetings and deliberations.

When lawmakers proposed in May 2025 requiring technology on AI chips so they could be tracked to deter smuggling, Nvidia pushed back. The company told lawmakers’ offices that the idea would be all but impossible to implement, and “defy the laws of physics,” according to a Senate aide. A few months later the company announced that it was releasing its own tracking software.
“We knew from that moment that they’re not going to be very honest in their dealings with us and Congress,” said the aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private meetings.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

To a growing number of officials in Washington, restricting exports of powerful AI chips is a matter of national security — a means to keeping America’s edge in a technology poised to remake the competition between the world’s two superpowers.

news.title: US ports face cyber attack onslaught as hackers target vital trade routes
news.title_en: US ports face cyber attack onslaught as hackers target vital trade routes

inline_images.caption: Cargo offloaded from a vessel in the Port of Corpus Christi. The port has ‘very analogue’ contingency plans should an attack breach its defences © Eddie Seal/Bloomberg
inline_images.alt: Cargo offloaded from a vessel in the Port of Corpus Christi. The port has ‘very analogue’ contingency plans should an attack breach its defences © Eddie Seal/Bloomberg

news.author: Martha Muir and Ella Lee
news.content_snippet: America's biggest crude oil export hub reports thousands of attempted hacks each day as shipping companies battle breaches
news.summary_en: Kent Britton, CEO of the Port of Corpus Christi, reported that the port faces thousands of daily network intrusion attempts. The FBI has warned that malicious actors are increasingly deploying an AI tool dubbed 'Artex' to automate the exploitation of software vulnerabilities within ports and shipping infrastructure, shifting from password spraying to sophisticated executive phishing.
paragraphs: Hackers are mounting an escalating cyber assault on US ports and cargo ships, bombarding vital arteries of global commerce with thousands of attempted attacks each day. The attacks have escalated sharply in recent months, with a wave of breaches targeting ports, oil tankers and shipping giants. The increasingly sophisticated threats are being carried out by cybercriminals and groups linked to hostile states, exposing vulnerabilities in the ageing networks that enable international commerce. At the Port of Corpus Christi in Texas, the largest US gateway for crude oil exports totalling around 2.3mn barrels per day, executives say hackers are probing their systems hundreds or even thousands of times a day, attempting to penetrate networks and trick employees into handing over access.The attacks can vary from automated attempts to guess passwords and overwhelm computer networks to more sophisticated intrusions meant to steal or erase data.

Experts link countries like Iran, North Korea and China to hacking operations targeting shipping infrastructure. Cybersecurity company Shieldworkz said Russia’s Noname057(16) threatened European operators this October — although groups route their operations through third-party countries.A wave of tech failures in recent weeks has shone a light on the vulnerability of other critical US digital infrastructure. A nationwide air traffic shutdown stranded hundreds of thousands of passengers a week ago, while a software glitch at Chase bank disrupted its banking systems on Monday, just days after Microsoft’s Outlook service went down for nearly 24 hours. None of these incidents have been linked to a cyber attack, but the chaos underlines the high stakes as rapid advances in AI could allow hackers to find and exploit vulnerabilities faster than companies can respond.
The FBI last week warned that hackers are using an AI tool named Artex to automate cyber attacks.

Corpus Christi port chief executive Kent Britton said attempted attacks have surged to a rate of “hundreds if not thousands” each day, from “known bad actor” states and organisations looking for high-profile targets. He declined to identify specific attackers.

Hackers are probing the port’s computer systems for weaknesses and sending fraudulent messages as senior executives to trick staff into allowing them access.“They’re poking at our systems and trying to find vulnerabilities,” Britton said. “With AI, it’ll only get more complicated.”

The threat is growing across the US. The US Coast Guard reported a 17 per cent increase in cyber maritime incidents last year and investigated cyber attacks on two US-bound oil tankers in August with the FBI.

The ships were carrying crude oil and liquefied petroleum gas from the Mediterranean to Galveston, Texas, when they were penetrated by hackers near the Strait of Gibraltar. Investigators have not publicly identified suspects.

The agencies said the joint offshore security boardings on August 21 and 24 were to “ensure integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised”.
Coast guard officers board a tanker that was compromised by a cyberattack as it was delivering into Galveston, Texas in August

Should hackers breach ports, they could paralyse trade, disrupt energy exports and put lives at risk at sea. In August, North Carolina Ports said its IT systems had experienced a cyber attack by an “outside actor”. Although it was contained a day later, gate openings were delayed and the port had to switch to manual processing.

The Port of Los Angeles said it thwarted 120mn attempted attacks this August, nearly double the monthly average in 2023. This includes automated attempts to breach networks, gather passwords and install malware.
Maersk reported an intrusion this month in which hackers stole data, but said its operations weren’t impacted. The shipping giant said the incident was not a ransomware attack.

news.title: States Sue SpaceX Over Grok Deepfakes
news.title_en: States Sue SpaceX Over Grok Deepfakes
news.author: Maddy Varner
news.content_snippet: The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia are suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX, alleging that the company violated consumer protection laws by lying to users about both the safety of its generative AI tools and how seriously the company took stopping child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII) from proliferating on its platforms. The suits follow a slew of other lawsuits against Musk’s companies around similar issues, including from the city of Baltimore and teens in
news.summary_en: The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia are suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX, alleging that the company violated consumer protection laws by lying to users about both the safety of its generative AI tools and how seriously the company took stopping child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII) from proliferating on its platforms. The suits follow a slew of other lawsuits against Musk’s companies around similar issues, including from the city of Baltimore and teens in
paragraphs: The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia are suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX, alleging that the company violated consumer protection laws by lying to users about both the safety of its generative AI tools and how seriously the company took stopping child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII) from proliferating on its platforms. The suits follow a slew of other lawsuits against Musk’s companies around similar issues, including from the city of Baltimore and teens in Tennessee.

The attorneys general are each filing their own complaints in their respective state courts—Virginia in the circuit court for the city of Richmond, and Oregon in Multnomah County circuit court. Both suits name SpaceX and X Corp., the SpaceX subsidiary responsible for the social media platform X. SpaceX acquired xAI, the Musk startup and parent company of X Corp., in February. In doing so it also took ownership of Grok, which is at the center of the allegations in the suit.

Last winter, the Grok chatbot made headlines after users on X started prompting it en masse to generate sexualized photos of women and minors. Even more disturbing AI-generated videos were later found on Grok’s website, including those showing female celebrities engaging in sexual activities.

The states allege that Grok’s creators ignored industry safety standards and intentionally implemented weak safeguards in an attempt to entice more people to use its “lagging product.” In all, as Virginia alleged in its complaint, the defendants saw “a market opportunity for more profits” in the generation of sexualized images of real people, including children, and “intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM.”

For example, the states say that Grok wasn’t subjected to enough third-party evaluations before releasing new models, and that Grok’s safety prompts included instructions to “assume good intent” and that the terms “teenage” and “girl” do “not necessarily imply underage.” They also allege that tens of thousands of reports were submitted without key information from xAI to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s CyberTipline, preventing the Center from being able to act on them 90 percent of the time.

In the complaints, the states say that Musk leaned into Grok’s “spicy mode” as a way to differentiate the model from its competitors and that this worked. They note, for example, that during the same time period that Grok’s ability to “undress” people was sparking international outrage, Musk posted about how Grok was “hitting #1 on the App Store in one country after another!” and discussing the chatbot’s “heavy usage growth.”

“It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material, because the lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug,” says Oregon attorney general Dan Rayfield in a statement.

Oregon and Virigina each filed their own “separate but similar actions” on Monday, but say they’ve been working in collaboration with each other. Both states retained Platkin LLP, a private law firm run by former New Jersey attorney general Matthew Platkin, to help litigate their cases.

Virginia attorney general Jay Jones says that both the collaboration and the decision to work with an outside firm came from trying to make the most of what they had. “Our offices are strapped. I wish I had all the resources in the world,” says Jones. “And so we oftentimes do partner with folks on the outside to make sure that we're pursuing the matters that are in the best interest of our constituencies.”

“I have a deep worry now into the future with this case and many others that we actually don't have the appropriate tools to deal with trillion-dollar corporations,” says Jones. “This is just a line item on a budget as the cost of doing business, right? Dealing with, you know, AG Jones and AG Rayfield. I think it's going to be real interesting to see how these cases go, because it's not just this, there's a lot of other things that we're looking at. How is this going to be grappled with as a society into the future?”

In its complaint, Virginia says that shortly before filing, its investigators tested Grok and found its image-generation safeguards were not only “inconsistent and ineffective,” but also taught users how to bypass moderation measures by explaining which words triggered its filters. When asked, the chatbot also helped state investigators draft prompts designed to avoid moderation and then carried out those prompts on request.
“At no point,” Virginia’s complaint says, “did Grok ask whether (a) the image uploaded was of a real person, or (b) whether the user had the person’s consent to use or modify the photo.”

news.title: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
news.title_en: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
news.author: James Temple
news.content_snippet:
Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slo
news.summary_en: Research by CarbonPlan suggests that 'Enhanced Rock Weathering' (ERW), a climate solution heavily backed by Google and Microsoft, faces significant scalability challenges. The study indicates that spreading basalt or olivine at levels required for climate impact may degrade soil health and decrease crop yields; scaling back applications to protect harvests would likely cap the method's CO2 removal potential to under 1 billion tons per year.
paragraphs: Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it , which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

“There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.

If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing. “Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.
So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).

Nov 23 (Reuters) - CrowdStrike said on Monday it would buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal that values the company at about $43.9 billion, deepening its push into network security and zero-trust services.

Zscaler shares jumped more than 13.4% in premarket trading, while CrowdStrike fell 5%.

news.summary_en: CrowdStrike has entered an all-stock acquisition agreement to purchase Zscaler in a deal valued at approximately $43.9 billion. The merger combines CrowdStrike’s endpoint security with Zscaler’s zero-trust network offerings to meet enterprise demand for vendor consolidation, with Zscaler shareholders receiving 1.135 CrowdStrike shares per share, resulting in existing CrowdStrike shareholders owning 84.1% of the new entity.
paragraphs: Zscaler shares jumped more than 13.4% in premarket trading, while CrowdStrike fell 5%.

The combination will create one of the world's largest pure-play cybersecurity providers as enterprise customers seek to reduce the number of security vendors they use, favoring providers that can deliver multiple products through a single relationship.

Shareholders of Zscaler will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share. The exchange ratio implies a value of about $260.41 per Zscaler share, representing a 34% premium to Zscaler's last close.
Existing CrowdStrike shareholders will own about 84.1% of the combined company after the transaction closes.
The companies expect to start with more than $10 billion in combined annual recurring revenue and target $1 billion of annualized revenue synergies.
This story was originally published November 23, 2026 at 5:44 AM.

paragraphs: Agon raises $70 million in Series A round to build Europe's defence AI lab Business Wire Mon, November 23, 2026 at 3:00 AM EST 6 min read The $70 million Series A round takes the total capital raised by Agon to $100 million, valuing the company at $450 million.
The round was led by Northzone, alongside other existing investors, including Lakestar, XYZ, Lux Capital, Global Founders Capital, and Speedinvest.
The UK Sovereign AI Fund and the National Security Strategic Investment Fund ('NSSIF') have invested together for the first time.
Agon Chairman David Helgason has increased his investment, while Roelof Botha has joined as a new investor.
The funding will accelerate Agon's mission to build Europe's foundational AI infrastructure and train the physical foundation models required for the era of agentic warfare.

LONDON, November 23, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Agon, the European defence AI company, has raised $70 million in its Series A round, to develop the infrastructure to train, validate and orchestrate autonomous defence systems.

The raise values the company at $450 million and is one of the largest European defence technology Series A rounds of 2026. It takes the total capital raised by Agon to $100 million, following its $30 million seed round earlier this year.

The round was led by Northzone, alongside other existing investors, including Lakestar, XYZ, Lux Capital, Global Founders Capital, Speedinvest, alongside new investment from the UK Sovereign AI Fund and NSSIF. This is the first time the two UK Government-backed strategic investment funds have invested together. The UK Sovereign AI Fund is Britain's sovereign venture fund dedicated to scaling British AI companies, while NSSIF is the UK Government's deep-tech venture capital fund for national security and defence, focused on strategically important dual-use technologies.

Agon Chairman David Helgason, founder of Unity Technologies and an existing investor, has increased his investment, while Roelof Botha, the former global leader of Sequoia Capital, and who serves on the boards of SpaceX and Unity, has joined as a new investor.
The investment will accelerate Agon's ambition to establish the European defence AI lab, developing the foundational infrastructure and AI models to create superior autonomous defence capabilities.

Tristam Constant, Co-Founder and CEO of Agon, said: "Europe is in an AI arms race as we enter the era of agentic warfare: intelligent agents and machines that will need to understand their environment, make decisions and adapt at a speed and scale that humans alone cannot match. We exist to build the sovereign infrastructure and AI foundation models to allow us to train, test, and evolve autonomous defence systems – in Europe, for Europe – to outperform adversary capabilities.

"Agon was born out of a project to bring together a coalition of European founders, operators, researchers, veterans, investors, and governments to build what we collectively believe to be urgently needed for our sovereignty and safety.

paragraphs: Becoming a programmer was, for me, a compromise. Midway through my junior year of college, it became clear that, as an international student from Korea, I likely wouldn’t be able to stay long after graduation unless I changed my major from philosophy to a STEM field that made me eligible for a visa extension. The obvious choice was computer science, which was already my minor.

The switch came with a sense of shame, which in retrospect had a whiff of melodrama. I suppose I was afflicted by what Ian McEwan once called “modern forms of snobbery” in describing a character who, after her bookish college education, came to consider “a man with a degree in chemistry incomplete as a human being.” Chemistry, computer science—same diff. It’s safe to say I did not have many friends in the CS department.

But I don’t think my squeamishness was entirely misplaced. In the post-Facebook-IPO ferment of the 2010s, this country’s computer science departments were newly flush with a certain breed of striver who in another era would’ve gone to Wall Street. My theory is that many in America who acquired a hostility toward technology acquired it by way of a hostility toward these upstarts. That is to say, they aren’t so much anti-technology as anti-technologist.

In any event, I half-assed my way through a good many CS assignments, which meant I was never in danger of going to grad school for AI. But by virtue of a robust public math education in Korea, my entry into the subject was, mercifully, not too bumpy. If anything, theoretical computer science and distributed systems seemed like a continuation of philosophy.

But I could not dispel the sense that programming was a frivolous waste of energy. Every line of code I had to read, every line of code I had to write, was a theft of the time I could’ve spent reading something I cared about. Perhaps it didn’t help that my first two languages were Java (hideous and tedious) and C (admirable but unforgiving). To this day, Java code is like a poisoned madeleine that brings back unwelcome memories.

After college, my visa dictated that I take a job directly tied to my major, and I found a tech company willing to sponsor my green card. The issue was, it could be any number of years until I got the green card—four, it’d turn out—so I figured I might as well find a way to make programming pleasurable.

The first couple of months on the job were joyless. I worked at a health care startup, which I thought gave me a serviceable sense of moral cover against the ongoing techlash and a way to indemnify myself later as a writer. But I liked my coworkers, some of whom also harbored artistic ambitions, and after work we’d regularly adjourn to literary events at the McNally Jackson, a block from our office.

Then, one day, I discovered a language called Haskell. I was tasked with rewriting a code base using a library that borrowed concepts from it. My vague impression of Haskell had been that it was a difficult language involving a branch of mathematics called category theory. There was something seductive about the intimidating aura around it, and when I tried my hand at writing basic programs, the language was indeed challenging, but appealingly so.

I started lurking in Haskell forums where researchers in the field of programming languages—“PL,” as it’s known—flaunted their lavish command of the language. PL researchers might as well be the poets of computer science: a small community of attentive monomaniacs who engaged in a largely unprofitable enterprise—a rarity in computer science—with all the attendant beef and infighting. The unprofitability meant that, unlike AI, the field had an incorruptible dignity to it.

Soon, to my surprise, I found myself programming outside work. After months of tinkering with Haskell, I discovered a book titled Writing a Compiler in Go. Turns out you could even invent a language yourself. I made a few toy languages, useless in practice but invaluable for demystifying how programming languages work.

There was also an oblique way coding could help writing. In Draft No. 4, John McPhee, the journalist’s journalist, says that he still uses an ancient text editor called Kedit, recommended to him in 1984 by a programmer at Princeton. (“I have never used a word processor,” he writes.) When I switched to a text editor myself, I could see why he’d stuck with it. With open source code, I could add silly but useful features, such as highlighting “TK”—a common shorthand in journalism for placeholder text—in a conspicuous color so that it was easy to locate later.
If nothing else, I came to appreciate that programming was a reliable way to enter that elusive mode called flow, a state in which we’re somehow forgetful and alert at once.

news.title: Trump hosts crypto traders as demand for his meme coin fades
news.title_en: Trump hosts crypto traders as demand for his meme coin fades
news.author: Isaac Arnsdorf
news.content_snippet:
In a reception room here where chandeliers abounded and women less so, top collectors of President Donald Trump’s novelty crypto token gathered to graze on fall harvest salad and filet mignon.

Some wore rented tuxes. At least one wore a red cap. A pump-up dancer in a Trump mask greeted them. VIP guests received gold-tone Trump diver watches and Trump-branded “Victory” fragrances at his Northern Virginia golf club, where they rubbed shoulders with retired athletes Floyd Mayweather and Tristan Th
news.summary_en: Former U.S. President Donald Trump hosted a crypto investor reception at his Northern Virginia golf club, aiming to re-engage high-net-worth holders and revive the market interest in his meme coins. Trump explicitly called for Congress to enact a federal regulatory framework for digital assets, attempting to align his political agenda with the industry's push for legal clarity.
paragraphs: In a reception room here where chandeliers abounded and women less so, top collectors of President Donald Trump’s novelty crypto token gathered to graze on fall harvest salad and filet mignon.

Some wore rented tuxes. At least one wore a red cap. A pump-up dancer in a Trump mask greeted them. VIP guests received gold-tone Trump diver watches and Trump-branded “Victory” fragrances at his Northern Virginia golf club, where they rubbed shoulders with retired athletes Floyd Mayweather and Tristan Thompson. Mentalist Lior Suchard claimed to read their minds.

Trump spoke for about 40 minutes. He predicted Wall Street would increasingly embrace crypto currencies and called for Congress to pass legislation establishing federal rules for digital assets — a measure that previously failed because Democrats objected to ethics exceptions for Trump and his family.
The biggest political news to start your morning. Sign up for free

He took questions from the group, including from a Chinese woman who asked for his favorite Chinese dish. He didn’t specify. He also sidestepped a question about how Viktor Orban’s loss in Hungary would affect the U.S. relationship with that country. He praised Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and declined to criticize Elon Musk for disavowing MAGA. He repeated that he would support former CEO Jensen Huang returning to Nvidia.

In response to a question about the situation in Haiti, Trump began criticizing Somali immigrants in Minnesota. And when one attendee urged Trump to run for a third term, he said the Constitution was clear that he could not.

The value of Trump’s meme coin has crashed, as most meme coins do. The digital assets are a way of monetizing attention, usually highest at their debut. This dinner was an effort to rustle up more interest, but a Washington Post analysis showed a seat could be secured for as little as $518, compared to $55,000 for the first gala in May 2025.
In the interim, his popularity plummeted, young men deserted him, and his party suffered its biggest midterms defeat in 52 years.
While most investors in the coin lost money, Trump reported earning $635 million from the meme coin last year.

When Trump announced the venture on the cusp of his second inauguration, Democrats and ethics experts decried it as a cash grab that could present an opportunity for lobbyists and favor-seekers to pay him off. The venture has been enormously lucrative for Trump, though the feared market for presidential influence is less clear. The buyers have been mostly Trump fans and crypto enthusiasts, sometimes both, according to attendees. Organizers and attendees said no one received individual time with the president at Sunday’s event.

The meme coin was the latest thing — this time a virtual one — for Trump to put his name on and sell, coming after skyscrapers, steaks, wine, casinos, clubs, neckties, vodka, a magazine, an airline, gold sneakers and a business seminar that paid $25 million to settle fraud claims. A company called Celebration Cards pays Trump to use his name for the crypto venture.

“Nobody seemed disappointed about the midterms or the price of the token,” said Morten Christensen, a crypto investor who attended Sunday’s dinner and met people there from countries including China, India, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom and Ukraine. “It was fun to be there.”

news.title: Behind China’s A.I. Anxieties, Fear of a Nuclear Checkmate
news.title_en: Behind China’s A.I. Anxieties, Fear of a Nuclear Checkmate

news.author: Chris Buckley
news.content_snippet:
When Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader, set about expanding China’s nuclear forces a decade ago, his goal was to ensure that enough missiles could survive an initial attack so Beijing could deliver a devastating counterattack.

That ability to withstand a strike and hit back would deter any enemy from risking nuclear blackmail or war against China in the first place, Chinese strategists have said.

But now, researchers in the Chinese military worry that American advances in artificial intelligence
news.summary_en: Researchers at the Academy of Military Science in Beijing warn that the U.S. integration of AI into nuclear decision-making could compress response times from 15-30 minutes to under 90 seconds. This capability sparks concerns that U.S. forces may achieve superior precision in detecting and neutralizing Chinese nuclear assets, thereby undermining Beijing's second-strike deterrence.
paragraphs: When Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader, set about expanding China’s nuclear forces a decade ago, his goal was to ensure that enough missiles could survive an initial attack so Beijing could deliver a devastating counterattack.
That ability to withstand a strike and hit back would deter any enemy from risking nuclear blackmail or war against China in the first place, Chinese strategists have said.

But now, researchers in the Chinese military worry that American advances in artificial intelligence could weaken Beijing’s nuclear hand in a crisis or conflict. They have been warning that artificial intelligence could make it easier for U.S. forces to find and wipe out Chinese nuclear missiles, giving Washington a menacing advantage.

The worries over A.I. complicate the growing nuclear tensions between Washington and Beijing, and could make China more reluctant to consider limits to its smaller arsenal. At a summit on Thursday, Mr. Xi, President Trump and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia spoke of reducing nuclear risks. But Mr. Xi has shown no interest in Mr. Trump’s calls for China to join arms control commitments.

A review of more than 100 recent studies by Chinese civilian and military researchers, as well as interviews with experts and former U.S. officials, points to a deep wariness in China about the American pursuit of A.I. in nuclear systems. At the same time, Chinese military institutes are also exploring how A.I. could make Chinese missiles harder to detect and knock from the sky.

China, the United States and Russia use radars, satellites and sensors to monitor each other’s nuclear weapons. Breakthroughs in A.I. could help create technology to detect, track and strike nuclear weapons more quickly and accurately. Experts in China worry that it could lag the United States in applying such advances.
A study from China’s top military institute described a scenario in which artificial intelligence accelerated U.S. actions in a crisis to mere moments, potentially overwhelming slower rivals.

“By embedding A.I. and other technologies into nuclear decision-making systems, the United States could compress the decision-making process from the traditional 15 to 30 minutes to 90 seconds or less, drastically increasing the speed of response,” two researchers from the Academy of Military Science in Beijing wrote in an overview of global nuclear trends published several months ago.

China has about 620 nuclear warheads that could be delivered by land- or submarine-based missiles, or by bombers, the Federation of American Scientists estimates. China’s arsenal is widely forecast to grow to about 1,000 warheads by 2030. (The United States and Russia each have around 1,800 nuclear warheads deployed for missiles and bombers, with thousands more stockpiled.)

China fears that A.I. advances could enable the United States “to rapidly engage in strikes as soon as something pops out from a hiding spot or mobilizes,” said Gerald C. Brown, a former analyst with the State Department who studies China’s nuclear strategy. “Basically, in their view, it could make survivability a lot more difficult.”

China’s missile force is closely watching the U.S. Strategic Command, which controls nuclear missiles and has said that it wants to use A.I. to enhance “decision-making capabilities.” Chinese military analysts are also studying how American conventional forces use A.I. to coordinate operations and pick targets.

The U.S. edge in making advanced chips is adding to Chinese concerns that the United States can move faster to incorporate A.I. into its military, including in nuclear-related systems, said Jacob Stokes, a senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security in Washington.

news.author: Bloomberg
news.content_snippet: A bipartisan group of US governors is urging Washington to set rules for the most powerful artificial intelligence systems …
news.summary_en: California Governor Gavin Newsom released a framework for AI governance, proposing baseline safety standards, mandatory third-party audits, emergency shutdown authorities, and limits on recursive self-improvement. The initiative aims to fill federal regulatory voids by imposing legal oversight on AI models with extreme catastrophic risk potential.
paragraphs: California Governor Gavin Newsom posted on X that President Donald Trump has failed America on AI safety and that the state is moving forward with mandatory safety standards and real accountability, according to the message, which shared a video and linked to new recommendations for California’s AI framework. The post from California drew hundreds of replies, with many users pointing to Newsom’s 2024 veto of a major AI safety bill and the state’s record on large projects, while experts connected to the recommendations offered support for the proposals.

The video shows Newsom seated at a table in a suit, speaking to the camera. He states that “two-thirds of all the large AI companies in terms of market cap are in the state of California,” calling the state “the center of this debate” and “the center of the responsibility to address” the issue “in the absence of any federal leadership.”

He refers to recent incidents at Microsoft, the FAA, the NSA, banks, and Apple, asking, “Is this all coincidental?” and whether “there’s no one at the helm taking responsibility.” He adds that the administration’s main step has been “a desire to preempt states like California to actually create guardrails.”

The remarks accompany the November 18 release of recommendations from the California Governor’s Office to strengthen the state’s AI framework. These include baseline safety standards, mandatory third-party oversight, emergency shutdown authority, and limits on recursive self-improvement.
The proposals follow a September executive order and have not yet been enacted as law. Newsom vetoed SB 1047 in 2024, which would have required testing of large models for catastrophic risks.

Some users criticized Newsom’s record in California, with one writing, “Gavin Newsom has FAILED California on literally everything,” and another stating, “You can’t spell CATASTROPHE without CA. California is a 24/7 dumpster fire.”
Others focused on his earlier veto, noting, “This is exactly the problem: big talk about AI regulation, but when SB 1047 reached his desk, Newsom vetoed it.”

A number of replies questioned the state’s ability to manage the issue, including comments such as, “You are a failure to Californians,” and “Gavin can’t even keep the storm drains functional. Everything Gavin does turns into disaster.”

Experts tied to the recommendations offered a different view. Alondra Nelson, a former acting director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, said, “That irresponsible culture cannot continue. I was proud to work with Governor Newsom and his team to advance the same standard that Americans rightfully expect from every other sector: no experimenting on the public.”

Jason Goldman, who served as the first White House Chief Digital Officer, stated, “This report tackles the hardest open questions in AI safety regulation, including how emergency shutdown of a frontier model would work in practice.”
The exchange adds another moment to the ongoing debate over who should set rules for artificial intelligence as California advances its recommendations and federal policy remains limited.

paragraphs: Chinese physical AI startup Simplexity Robotics received $100 million in a funding round led by Jack Ma-backed Ant Group Co., marking one of the fintech giant's most significant bets on next-generation embodied intelligence.

The Suzhou-based robotics pioneer issued convertible preferred shares in the transaction, valuing the embodied AI maker at a premium following successful field trials of its industrial-grade bipedal and dexterous mobile manipulation units.

Ant Group's strategic investment underscores a broader push across China's technology sector into physical artificial intelligence, where frontier software models are integrated with advanced actuators, sensory end-effectors, and spatial navigation hardware.

Simplexity Robotics plans to deploy the capital expansion toward accelerating mass production of its general-purpose humanoid platforms and expanding proprietary reinforcement learning foundation models for complex manufacturing assembly lines.

The deal positions Ant Group alongside major domestic cloud and venture capital players racing to secure foundational physical AI assets before Western competitors commercialize consumer-ready humanoid workforces.

news.summary_en: China has warned that it will take action to defend its interests after US President Donald Trump's administration introduced tougher restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips, escalating tensions over technology access just as the two countries prepare for high-level talks.The measures could also disrupt Southeast Asia's rapidly expanding technology industry, where billions of dollars are being invested in data centres powered by American-made processors.On Monday, 16 November
paragraphs: China has warned that it will take action to defend its interests after US President Donald Trump's administration introduced tougher restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips, escalating tensions over technology access just as the two countries prepare for high-level talks.The measures could also disrupt Southeast Asia's rapidly expanding technology industry, where billions of dollars are being invested in data centres powered by American-made processors.On Monday, 16 November, Washington announced that it would tighten controls on advanced semiconductors and overseas computing facilities that could give Chinese businesses access to restricted American technology, Reuters reported.On Tuesday, 17 November, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun condemned the restrictions as economic coercion, accusing Washington of interfering in normal trade and technological cooperation.

He said Beijing would take necessary measures to safeguard its legitimate and lawful rights and interests.Washington Targets Overseas Access to NVIDIA ChipsThe new regulations are intended to close a route through which Chinese companies have obtained access to powerful American processors without purchasing the hardware directly.

Although Washington already restricts sales of its most advanced AI chips to China, businesses there have been able to rent computing capacity from overseas data centres equipped with the technology.The latest restrictions require US export licences for covered advanced semiconductor shipments to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, countries Washington considers at higher risk of technology diversion.

The rule includes an exemption for shipments destined for US-headquartered companies, or businesses whose ultimate parent is based in the United States, provided specified reporting requirements are met.NVIDIA is particularly exposed because its processors are widely used to develop and train advanced AI systems.

The restrictions could complicate sales and infrastructure partnerships across the region, although the rules do not amount to a blanket prohibition on every shipment or data centre operation in the affected countries.Southeast Asia's $100 Billion AI Industry Faces UncertaintyThe market reaction was already apparent on Tuesday, 17 November, when investors sold shares in companies exposed to the region's data centre expansion.

Malaysia's MN Holdings and Critical Holdings each fell nearly 20 per cent, while YTL Power, an NVIDIA partner in AI infrastructure, dropped almost 10 per cent.The sell-off also spread to semiconductor suppliers and other technology-related companies across Asia, reflecting concerns about the potential impact of the new licensing requirements.The potential disruption is significant for a region that has attracted enormous investment in digital infrastructure.

Malaysia has recorded 385.7 billion ringgit (£71.5 billion) in data centre-related investments since 2021.Thailand, meanwhile, had attracted around $22.6 billion (£17.2 billion) in data centre investment by February 2026. Restrictions that delay equipment deliveries or make it harder to secure customers could undermine expansion plans and affect businesses supplying these facilities.Singapore Seeks Clarity From WashingtonSingapore is among the countries facing the new licensing requirements and has begun discussions with American officials about how the restrictions will be applied.

Its government said it was examining the regulations and assessing their implications for domestic businesses, while seeking arrangements that would allow legitimate companies to maintain access to advanced technology.Officials also stressed that Singapore would not tolerate businesses exploiting their presence in the country to evade foreign export restrictions.

The response reflects the challenge facing regional governments: protecting their growing technology industries while maintaining their relationships with Washington and complying with international trade requirements.

news.summary_en: London-based legal tech firm Alecto raised $20 million in a seed round led by Insight Partners. Founded by Will Rice, the firm aims to leverage AI to automate complex property conveyancing tasks in the UK, challenging traditional hourly billing models to improve transparency and consumer outcomes by 2027.
paragraphs: Alecto Conveyancing Ltd., a London-based artificial intelligence-native law firm, today announced it raised $20 million in seed funding led by Insight Partners to make the law more accessible to the general public.

Firstminute Capital, Blue Lion Global, Andrena Ventures, FJ Labs, Antiportfolio Ventures, the Rigby Group and Mischon de Reya LLP also joined in the round. Angel investors participating in the round included Octopus Group Chief Executive and founder Simon Rogerson and SwiftKey founder John Reynolds.

Founded in September 2025 by CEO Will Rice (pictured), a serial entrepreneur who previously built fintech mortgage lender Gen H, Alecto’s first service targets the United Kingdom conveyancing market, the legal work required to buy and sell property. Rice drew on his experience building a mortgage company and decided to focus initially on bringing more people into ownership. With that expertise, Alecto aims to use AI to help give everyday people greater access to the law.

Alecto argues that traditional legal services are starved, with too few qualified attorneys and too few hours a day. Billing is based on hours, not outcomes and the service model doesn’t lean toward customers; this leads to unpredictable costs and a process that leaves customers in the dark.

The law firm said it’s using AI and legal experts to explain opaque legal processes in plain language and help clients make informed decisions. The company intends to target the property conveyancing market, which represents almost $3.3 billion in the U.K. alone, and aims to become the number one leader in property legal services by 2027.

“For too long, the legal industry has expected customers to work on its terms; now, AI presents the opportunity to put the consumer in control,” Rice said. “People don’t want to buy a lawyer’s time; they want results. Alecto exists to make the law accessible to everyone, giving control back to the consumer.”

Consumer legal services in the U.K. value growth pushed revenue over £55 billion, around $72.5 billion, in 2026, according to a report from Research and Markets. Business and commercial practices lead with 51% market value, followed by growth in the injury and conveyancing law markets.

“Property is where we prove the model. We’re building the technology and operations to rapidly break into new countries and new areas of law,” Rice added. “Ultimately, access to exceptional legal support should not depend on how much money you have or how confidently you can navigate the system.”
